definition: In artificial intelligence, with implications for cognitive science, the frame problem describes an issue with using first-order logic to express facts about a robot in the world.
details: Representing the state of a robot with traditional first-order logic requires the use of many axioms that simply imply that things in the environment do not change arbitrarily. For example, Hayes describes a "block world" with rules about stacking blocks together. In a first-order logic system, additional axioms are required to make inferences about the environment (for example, that a block cannot change position unless it is physically moved). The frame problem is the problem of finding adequate collections of axioms for a viable description of a robot environment. John McCarthy and Patrick J. Hayes defined this problem in their 1969 article, Some Philosophical Problems from the Standpoint of Artificial Intelligence. In this paper, and many that came after, the formal mathematical problem was a starting point for more general discussions of the difficulty of knowledge representation for artificial intelligence. Issues such as how to provide rational default assumptions and what humans consider common sense in a virtual environment. explainer.lead: When a robot acts, most of the world stays the same. The frame problem is the difficulty of making a logical system account for that stability without endless rules, and it matters because a practical robot must reason about change without reconsidering everything it believes.

tiers.eli5: Imagine moving one toy block while everything else in your room stays put. A robot following strict logical rules may also need rules saying that the cup, the floor, and every other block did not move. The frame problem is about avoiding an endless list of these “nothing changed” rules.
tiers.practitioner: In a first-order-logic robot model, rules for an action's effects are not enough: the representation must also support inferences about which facts persist. A key pitfall is relying on ever-growing collections of frame axioms, while rational default assumptions and common-sense expectations remain difficult to represent. It also helps to distinguish representing local change from deciding which beliefs need updating.
tiers.paperLevel: John McCarthy and Patrick J. Hayes defined the problem in their 1969 article, Some Philosophical Problems from the Standpoint of Artificial Intelligence. Formally, the task is to find an adequate collection of first-order-logic axioms for a viable robot-environment description, including persistence conditions such as position(b, t+1) = position(b, t) unless b is physically moved. The broader problem extends to rational defaults, common sense, and limiting the beliefs that must be updated.

explainer.example: Suppose block A is moved onto block B while block C sits nearby. The action rule accounts for A's new position, but additional axioms are needed to infer that C has not moved and that blocks do not change position unless physically moved.

explainer.intuition: Describing what an action changes is only half the task; a reasoning system must also know that unrelated things stay unchanged.
howItWorks: Describe the robot and its environment as logical facts.
Add rules for actions, such as physically moving a block.
Add axioms supporting inferences about facts that remain unchanged.
Seek an adequate collection of axioms without allowing arbitrary environmental changes.
explainer.whyItMatters: The problem exposes a central difficulty in knowledge representation: making logical descriptions of action usable without explicitly restating every stable fact. It also connects formal reasoning to wider questions about defaults, common sense, and belief updating.
misconceptions: It is not just about describing what moves; the central difficulty is accounting for what does not change.
It is not merely a matter of counting axioms; broader versions concern defaults, common sense, and belief revision.
It is not confined to robots, since it also has implications for cognitive science and philosophy.
